title: Realism Was Forged in Trauma
gist: Reviewing David M. Sacks' biography 'The Realist', Jon Skolnik traces Hans Morgenthau's power-centric realism to his trauma as a Jewish youth in 1920s Coburg, and argues today's U.S. interventionism, including the Iran war, is not true Morgenthau realism but a trauma-driven distortion that turns 'national interest' into an empty signifier.

insights.claim: Enduring theories of power—Thucydides, Hobbes, Machiavelli, and Morgenthau—were often formulated by thinkers experiencing exile or powerlessness.
insights.speaker: Jon Skolnik
insights.so_what: Intellectual-history context for why realist frameworks emphasize vigilance and distrust of rules.
insights.quote: Some of the most enduring theories of power were born in its absence.

insights.claim: Morgenthau's experience of antisemitic abuse and Hitler's 1922 storm into Coburg with 800 stormtroopers taught him that powerless individuals could not rely on law or abstract ideals for protection, shaping a post-traumatic theory of power.
insights.speaker: Jon Skolnik
insights.so_what: Explains realism's core skepticism of rules-based orders.
insights.quote: He, and other powerless individuals, could not rely on the law or abstract ideals for protection.

insights.claim: Morgenthau's realism holds that nations pursue power above all, peace depends on a balance of power, moral values must align with national interest, security commitments are doubtful, and the world's default state is anarchy.
insights.speaker: Jon Skolnik
insights.so_what: A lens for reading great-power behavior and the fragility of alliance commitments.
insights.quote: The distribution of power,” as Morgenthau warned, “is always precarious.

themes.theme: Restraint as true realism: Vietnam and after

insights.claim: Morgenthau, though hawkish on Cuba, opposed U.S. intervention in Vietnam for two decades on narrow strategic grounds, arguing the U.S. should intervene only where national interest requires it and its power gives a chance of success.
insights.speaker: Jon Skolnik
insights.so_what: Realism, properly applied, is a doctrine of restraint rather than aggression.
insights.quote: If the United States applies this standard, it will intervene less and succeed more.

insights.claim: Aggression is not a good proxy for realism, which, as John Mearsheimer notes, is largely predicated on restraint; recent wars in Gaza, Ukraine, and Iran instead expose that the rules-based order is only as strong as those who abide by it.
insights.speaker: Jon Skolnik
insights.so_what: Expect continued erosion of rules-based constraints on great powers, sustaining geopolitical risk premia.

themes.theme: Trauma and the hollowing of 'national interest'

insights.claim: A key weakness of realism is the malleability of 'national interest', which collective trauma like 9/11 can stretch until distant threats seem existentially urgent.
insights.speaker: Jon Skolnik
insights.so_what: Watch for threat-inflation rhetoric as a leading indicator of new or expanded military commitments.

insights.claim: The author contends that if realism predominates among U.S. policymakers today, it is a distorted form in which national trauma has turned national interest into an empty signifier used for vengeful wish fulfillment, with power pursued for its own sake.
insights.speaker: Jon Skolnik
